stem: A 44-year-old with a prosthetic aortic valve has persistent fever and two blood cultures growing Staphylococcus aureus. TTE shows no vegetation.
ask: Which action is MOST appropriate?
options: Exclude endocarditis because TTE is normal
Arrange urgent transoesophageal echocardiography and infectious diseases/cardiology assessment
Start oral antibiotics alone for five days
Repeat cultures in six months only
Remove the prosthetic valve without further assessment
explanations: TTE can miss vegetations, particularly around prosthetic valves.
TEE is more sensitive for prosthetic valve endocarditis, and S. aureus bacteraemia needs urgent management.
Short oral therapy is inadequate for suspected endocarditis.
Delayed cultures miss persistent bacteraemia.
Surgery depends on complications and specialist assessment.
pearl: S. aureus bacteraemia plus a prosthetic valve has a high threshold for endocarditis evaluation.
pivot: New heart failure, abscess or conduction block raises concern for a perivalvular complication.

stem: A 68-year-old with diabetes presents with fever, confusion, neck stiffness and a purpuric rash. Lumbar puncture will be delayed by resuscitation and imaging.
ask: What is the MOST appropriate antimicrobial approach?
options: Wait for CSF results before antibiotics
Take blood cultures promptly, then give empiric IV antibiotics without waiting for LP
Give topical antibiotics only
Wait for the rash to disappear
Start antiviral treatment alone
explanations: Treatment delay increases mortality in bacterial meningitis.
Blood cultures and immediate age-appropriate empiric IV antibiotics are required; add other therapy based on guideline.
Topical treatment cannot treat invasive infection.
Rash resolution is irrelevant.
Antivirals alone do not cover meningococcal or pneumococcal meningitis.
pearl: Never delay meningitis antibiotics for CT or LP.
pivot: Where indicated, give adjunct dexamethasone with or just before first antibiotic dose.

stem: A 61-year-old has fatigue, jaundice and dark urine. Hb 72 g/L, LDH elevated, haptoglobin undetectable and direct antiglobulin test positive for IgG. Blood film has spherocytes.
ask: Which treatment is MOST appropriate for likely warm autoimmune haemolytic anaemia?
options: Oral iron alone
Systemic glucocorticoids after specialist assessment, plus supportive care
Plasma exchange for every patient
Immediate splenectomy in every patient
Aspirin monotherapy
explanations: Iron does not correct immune red cell destruction.
Warm AIHA is commonly treated initially with glucocorticoids, with transfusion support if needed.
Plasma exchange is not routine first-line therapy for warm AIHA.
Splenectomy may be considered later in selected refractory cases.
Aspirin does not suppress antibody-mediated haemolysis.
pearl: DAT-positive IgG haemolysis with spherocytes suggests warm AIHA.
pivot: Cold agglutinin disease differs in complement involvement and treatment strategy.

stem: A 40-year-old develops fever, confusion and petechiae. Hb 78 g/L, platelets 12 × 10⁹/L, creatinine mildly elevated; smear shows schistocytes and coagulation studies are near normal.
ask: What is the MOST appropriate immediate treatment?
options: Platelet transfusions routinely before any other management
Urgent plasma exchange with specialist-directed immunosuppression for suspected TTP
Wait for ADAMTS13 results before treatment
Treat with oral iron and discharge
Give warfarin
explanations: Platelet transfusion may worsen thrombosis and is generally reserved for life-threatening haemorrhage.
TTP is life-threatening microangiopathy needing urgent plasma exchange and specialist treatment.
ADAMTS13 confirmation must not delay treatment.
Iron does not treat microvascular thrombi.
Warfarin does not resolve TTP.
pearl: Schistocytes + thrombocytopenia + neurological symptoms: treat presumed TTP before confirmatory test.
pivot: DIC usually produces abnormal PT/aPTT and fibrinogen abnormalities.

stem: A 25-year-old with sickle cell disease has severe bone pain and fever, then develops chest pain, hypoxia and a new pulmonary infiltrate.
ask: What is the MOST likely complication?
options: Uncomplicated pain crisis alone
Acute chest syndrome
Asthma without another diagnosis
Stable chronic anaemia
Simple viral rhinitis
explanations: New hypoxia and infiltrate extend beyond a typical pain crisis.
Acute chest syndrome requires oxygen, antibiotics, analgesia and transfusion consideration.
Asthma may coexist but does not explain the full syndrome.
Baseline anaemia alone does not cause new infiltrate.
Rhinitis is not a sufficient explanation.
pearl: Sickle cell + new lung infiltrate and respiratory symptoms = acute chest syndrome.
pivot: Rapid deterioration or severe hypoxaemia may necessitate exchange transfusion.

stem: A 64-year-old suddenly loses painless vision in one eye. Fundoscopy shows a pale retina with a cherry-red fovea; there is no retinal detachment.
ask: Which action is MOST appropriate?
options: Arrange routine optometry next month
Activate urgent stroke/ophthalmology evaluation for central retinal artery occlusion
Treat as conjunctivitis with drops
Advise eye exercises
Reassure because there is no eye pain
explanations: Retinal arterial occlusion is time-critical, not routine follow-up.
CRAO is a retinal infarction needing emergent vascular and ophthalmic assessment.
Conjunctivitis causes discomfort and discharge, not profound sudden loss.
Exercises do not restore arterial perfusion.
Painlessness is characteristic of vascular loss.
pearl: CRAO is an eye stroke; evaluate embolic sources and giant cell arteritis when relevant.
pivot: Flashes and a curtain-like field defect instead suggest retinal detachment.

stem: A 67-year-old has temporal headache, jaw claudication and transient monocular vision loss. ESR 96 mm/hr; temporal artery is tender.
ask: What is MOST appropriate immediately?
options: Wait for biopsy before starting treatment
Begin high-dose glucocorticoids urgently and arrange specialist workup
Prescribe topical ocular lubricants alone
Offer reassurance for migraine
Start anticoagulation as sole therapy
explanations: Delay risks permanent bilateral visual loss.
Suspected giant cell arteritis with visual symptoms requires immediate systemic steroids without waiting for biopsy.
Lubricants cannot prevent ischaemia.
Jaw claudication and raised inflammatory markers make benign migraine less likely.
Anticoagulation does not treat vessel inflammation.
pearl: Visual symptoms in suspected GCA make treatment a time-critical emergency.
pivot: Ultrasound or biopsy can support diagnosis but should not postpone steroids.

stem: A 38-year-old has fever, unilateral sore throat, muffled hot-potato voice, trismus and uvula deviated away from a bulging tonsil.
ask: Which management is MOST appropriate?
options: Discharge on throat lozenges alone
Urgent assessment for peritonsillar abscess drainage and antibiotics, with airway evaluation
Perform blind repeated throat swabbing
Give long-term proton pump inhibitor alone
Wait four weeks for outpatient ENT review
explanations: Symptoms suggest suppurative infection with possible airway risk.
Peritonsillar abscess usually requires drainage assessment and appropriate antibiotics.
Blind manipulation risks harm and does not manage collection.
Reflux treatment does not resolve abscess.
Delay risks spread and airway compromise.
pearl: Trismus + unilateral bulge + uvular deviation suggests quinsy.
pivot: Bilateral swelling with drooling or stridor requires emergency airway attention.

stem: A 7-year-old has ear pain and fever, then swelling, redness and tenderness behind the pinna with protrusion of the ear. Otoscopy suggests acute otitis media.
ask: What complication should be suspected and managed urgently?
options: Uncomplicated cerumen impaction
Acute mastoiditis requiring hospital ENT assessment and IV antibiotics
Allergic rhinitis
Otitis externa without deeper infection
Benign ear wax build-up
explanations: Wax does not cause systemic illness and postauricular swelling.
Postauricular erythema and displacement of the pinna after AOM indicate mastoiditis.
Rhinitis does not cause local mastoid tenderness.
Otitis externa localises to external canal inflammation.
This presentation is not benign.
pearl: Pinna pushed forward with postauricular swelling is classic mastoiditis.
pivot: Neurological changes or facial palsy suggest intracranial or nerve complications.

stem: A 22-year-old sustains a tibial fracture and has escalating pain despite opioids. Pain is severe on passive toe extension; the leg is tense, but pulses remain palpable.
ask: Which management is MOST appropriate?
options: Discharge because pulses are present
Immediate orthopaedic assessment for compartment syndrome and urgent fasciotomy if indicated
Elevate the limb very high and observe overnight
Give high-dose aspirin as definitive therapy
Delay assessment until X-ray is repeated tomorrow
explanations: Pulses may persist until late in compartment syndrome.
Disproportionate pain and passive stretch pain demand urgent diagnosis and decompression.
Excessive elevation reduces perfusion pressure and delays treatment.
Aspirin cannot relieve raised compartment pressure.
Delayed treatment risks irreversible necrosis.
pearl: Do not rely on absent pulses to diagnose compartment syndrome.
pivot: In an obtunded patient, compartment pressure measurement can support diagnosis when examination is unreliable.

stem: A 75-year-old falls and has hip pain, a shortened externally rotated leg and inability to bear weight. Initial AP pelvis X-ray is normal.
ask: Which next investigation is MOST appropriate if clinical suspicion remains high?
options: Discharge because radiographs are normal
Urgent MRI hip for occult fracture, or CT if MRI unavailable
Routine lumbar puncture
Bone scan after three months
Repeat plain radiograph in six weeks only
explanations: Radiographically occult hip fractures occur and need exclusion.
MRI is most sensitive for an occult proximal femoral fracture; timely CT can be an alternative.
CSF testing is irrelevant.
Late scans delay safe management.
Waiting risks displacement and complications.
pearl: A normal X-ray does not exclude fracture in someone unable to bear weight after a fall.
pivot: If advanced imaging confirms no fracture, evaluate alternative musculoskeletal or pelvic causes.

stem: A 58-year-old has atraumatic hot swollen knee with fever 39°C. Joint aspirate is turbid with neutrophils 95%; blood cultures are pending.
ask: What is the MOST appropriate management?
options: Intra-articular corticosteroid injection first
Urgent antibiotics after prompt cultures/aspiration and orthopaedic washout assessment
Oral NSAIDs alone
Elective review in two months
High-impact exercises to prevent stiffness
explanations: Steroid injection into infection can worsen it.
Septic arthritis threatens cartilage and needs urgent antimicrobials and drainage assessment.
Analgesia alone does not control infection.
Delay risks irreversible joint destruction.
Exercise does not treat a septic joint.
pearl: A hot swollen joint is septic arthritis until proved otherwise.
pivot: Crystal arthropathy and infection can coexist, so crystals do not rule out sepsis.

stem: A competent 58-year-old with severe anaemia refuses a recommended blood transfusion after a clear explanation of benefits and risks. He understands the consequences and communicates a stable decision.
ask: Which is the MOST appropriate response?
options: Transfuse against his will because it is lifesaving
Respect informed refusal, document capacity and discussion, and explore acceptable alternatives
Ask family to override his decision
Sedate him to give blood covertly
Declare incapacity solely because his choice is medically risky
explanations: Competent refusal must not be overridden solely to achieve benefit.
Autonomy requires respecting capacity-based refusal, with documentation and alternatives.
Family cannot override a competent patient's decision.
Covert treatment violates consent.
An unwise choice does not by itself indicate lack of capacity.
pearl: Capacity is decision-specific and assesses understanding, retention, weighing and communication.
pivot: If a patient lacks capacity during an emergency, substitute decision-making law and best-interest principles apply.

stem: A 67-year-old with type 2 diabetes has eGFR 32 mL/min/1.73m², UACR 45 mg/mmol, HbA1c 7.9%, BP 146/88. He takes metformin and an ACE inhibitor.
ask: Which addition is MOST supported for kidney and cardiovascular protection, subject to contraindications?
options: Routine systemic corticosteroid
SGLT2 inhibitor at an evidence-supported eGFR threshold
Stop all antihypertensives
Start NSAID daily
Add a sulfonylurea as the only renal protective measure
explanations: Steroids worsen glycaemic control and do not protect diabetic kidney disease.
SGLT2 inhibitors reduce CKD progression and cardiovascular events in eligible patients.
BP control and RAAS blockade are important.
NSAIDs may worsen renal function.
Sulfonylureas lower glucose but do not offer comparable renal benefits.
pearl: Albuminuric CKD shifts diabetes treatment toward organ protection, not only HbA1c.
pivot: Acute illness, ketoacidosis risk and volume status can require temporary SGLT2 interruption.

stem: A 56-year-old asymptomatic person asks for a screening test that finds many indolent tumours but has not shown reduced overall mortality. False positives lead to biopsies.
ask: Which concept MOST directly describes detection of disease that would never cause symptoms or harm?
options: Lead-time bias only
Overdiagnosis
Confounding by indication
Selection bias only
Incidence rate ratio
explanations: Lead-time bias creates apparent survival gain without changing death timing but is not identical to detecting harmless disease.
Overdiagnosis is the detection of abnormalities that would not have caused clinical problems.
Confounding relates to nonrandom treatment selection.
Selection bias is not the specific harm described.
Incidence ratio is a statistic, not the concept.
pearl: Screening benefit must be weighed against overdiagnosis and overtreatment.
pivot: False positives are separate from overdiagnosis: they do not represent true disease.

stem: An 81-year-old with advanced dementia has aspiration pneumonia. The family demands a feeding tube to prevent all future aspiration, though the patient's advance care plan favours comfort.
ask: Which discussion point is MOST accurate?
options: Tube feeding completely eliminates aspiration risk
Tube feeding does not reliably prevent aspiration pneumonia in advanced dementia; use shared goals-of-care planning
Advance care plans have no relevance
Feeding tubes always improve survival in this setting
Family preferences automatically supersede every documented patient wish
explanations: Aspiration of saliva and reflux can occur despite feeding tubes.
Evidence does not show routine tube feeding prevents aspiration pneumonia in advanced dementia; discuss comfort feeding and values.
Prior patient preferences are highly relevant.
Survival benefit is not reliably established for routine tube feeding in advanced dementia.
Decision-making must consider prior expressed wishes and local legal framework.
pearl: Distinguish aspiration risk from nutritional intake; a tube may not solve both.
pivot: Temporary tube feeding can have a role for selected reversible conditions with different goals.

stem: A 28-year-old has fever, lumbar pain and new leg weakness two weeks after an epidural procedure. Examination shows sensory loss and urinary retention.
ask: Which is the MOST appropriate response?
options: Give analgesia and outpatient review next month
Urgent spinal MRI, blood cultures if feasible, empiric IV antibiotics and specialist surgical assessment
Treat as muscular strain only
Perform high-velocity spinal manipulation
Start oral steroids alone without investigating infection
explanations: Neurological deficits after possible spinal infection require emergency assessment.
Spinal epidural abscess threatens paralysis; prompt imaging, antimicrobials and decompression review are critical.
Muscular strain cannot explain urinary retention and fever.
Manipulation may worsen injury.
Steroids alone can mask infection and delay care.
pearl: Classic triad is often incomplete: fever plus back pain plus deficit is enough to act.
pivot: Stable patients without neurological deficits may allow a more controlled diagnostic sequence.

stem: A 34-year-old recently returned from a malaria-endemic region with fever, jaundice, confusion, and thrombocytopenia. Thin smear shows Plasmodium falciparum parasitaemia 8%.
ask: Which management is MOST appropriate?
options: Oral chloroquine and home observation
Urgent parenteral artesunate with intensive supportive care for severe malaria
Wait for repeat smear before treatment
Give oral doxycycline alone
Use antipyretics only
explanations: Chloroquine resistance and severe manifestations make this inadequate.
Cerebral symptoms and high parasitaemia indicate severe falciparum malaria requiring immediate IV artesunate per protocol.
Life-threatening malaria should not wait.
Doxycycline alone is not adequate acute severe malaria therapy.
Supportive antipyretics do not treat parasitaemia.
pearl: Falciparum malaria can rapidly cause encephalopathy, acidosis and organ failure.
pivot: Uncomplicated malaria can be treated with appropriate oral combination therapy based on species and region.

stem: A 45-year-old with HIV has progressive dyspnoea, dry cough, fever, SpO₂ 88% and bilateral diffuse interstitial infiltrates. CD4 count 58 cells/µL; Pneumocystis infection is suspected.
ask: Which therapy is MOST appropriate?
options: Oral amoxicillin as sole treatment
High-dose co-trimoxazole and assess need for adjunct corticosteroids based on oxygenation
Stop all antimicrobial therapy until bronchoscopy
Nebulised salbutamol alone
Give oseltamivir as definitive therapy
explanations: Amoxicillin does not target Pneumocystis.
Co-trimoxazole is first-line; moderate–severe hypoxaemia can warrant adjunct steroids.
Diagnostic confirmation should not delay treatment in high-likelihood severe disease.
Bronchodilator alone does not eradicate infection.
Oseltamivir treats influenza, not Pneumocystis.
pearl: PJP is associated with CD4 below 200 and disproportionate hypoxaemia.
pivot: PaO₂ below 70 mmHg on room air or A–a gradient ≥35 mmHg supports adjunct corticosteroids.

stem: A junior doctor notices a colleague gave ten times the intended dose of an opioid; the patient is drowsy with RR 7/min. The colleague asks for secrecy to protect their career.
ask: Which action is MOST appropriate?
options: Keep quiet if the patient later wakes
Immediately treat the patient, escalate to senior staff and follow transparent incident reporting and disclosure processes
Wait until the next morning to document
Delete the medication chart entry
Blame nursing staff to avoid conflict
explanations: Recovery does not excuse withholding safety concerns.
Patient stabilisation, honest escalation and transparent reporting protect the patient and support systems improvement.
Delay permits preventable harm.
Altering records is dishonest and dangerous.
Blame undermines just culture and safety.
pearl: Duty of candour begins with safeguarding the patient and accurate disclosure.
pivot: Near misses should also be reported through appropriate safety systems.
